guest.bio_context: John Warburton started in the fenestration industry in the mid-1980s at a small PVC window fabricator in Lancashire, where he learned manufacturing from start to finish. He progressed through various roles including field technician at Profile 22, exports manager during the global recession, technical manager at Commolin for eight to nine years, and held multiple positions at Vika and Epwin in product development and sales. He later joined the Building Research Establishment (BRE) in Watford to help set up certification schemes for windows and doors, before joining ER Certification as a small company initially, purchasing the business from founder Bill Keaton three years prior to this interview.

context.transcript_excerpt: I'm Richard Lannan, Roger Canan, and this is the Glazing Insider Industry Podcast. John, welcome to the podcast. Thank you for coming on. Thank you. How did you get into the fenestration world? I started back in the mid-80s at a small fabricator in Lancashire making PVC windows, in the early days of PVC windows. And I just fell into the job because I needed a job. I'd dropped out of college. I didn't know what I was going to do. I thought about joining the Navy. They didn't want me. So I found a job and spent my first morning on a Elomatic DG79 profile saw, cutting profile. And I stayed in that factory for 18 months. I progressed through into the office, order processing, purchasing, laying out bays. And it was a real good grounding. That first 18 months manufacturing where I learned manufacturing from start to finish. These days you go in factories, people stay on one job, never move. They don't learn how to make a window. They learn how to do one part of it. In those days, we learned everything. We had no support from system houses. There was no technical manuals. There's nothing to learn from. It was trial and error. But we did pretty well. From there, like I say, I went through the office. I learned order processing, purchasing. We expanded. We built conservatories with no concept of how they should be built. But we learned, again, trial and error. And I was there about nine years. I then was young, ambitious. I'd done a marketing course at night school. Uh, and I really wanted to be a salesman. So I got a job, um, with profile 22 as a field technician going, supporting fabricators in the field. I did that for 12 months and then they offered me a sales position. So that was great. Um, 12 months after that, another position came up, which was exports. Um, it was a difficult time. Um, it was, uh, you know, global economy had crashed global recession. and this sort of picked on me, I think, because I was a bit technical and a bit sales and I could look after the customers we got. But in the 18 months I was in that role, we did really well. We got new customers on in Ukraine, in America, in quite a few places. Never got an order from an existing customer, but we got quite a few new ones on. So that was okay, but a big new customer in China. but I went to China and I thought there's not a lot of future in shipping profiles halfway around the world to a country that's just going to copy what you've got and do it equally as well so um position came up within profile 22 back in the UK um organization uh I applied for that I was successful and so I was technical support manager there and um then I got an opportunity to move to Commolin um and that was probably one of the best moves i was technical manager in the uk for comlin for eight nine years um and i learned a lot more there in terms of system design uh extrusion heavily involved in development of new systems several new systems through through that period um a lot of upheaval it was a roller coaster commonly went bust at that point taken over a couple of times the organization changed considerably and yeah, I was there for quite some time. We merged with KBE and Trocal and the organisation changed. I wasn't as happy as I had been and I got an approach from Vika to go back into sales. So I explained to them at the time, yeah, I'm not really a salesman and they said it doesn't matter. Get here and you can do lots of stuff. There's lots of scope. So I went and interestingly, the guy that had actually approached me and taken me on had left the company before I started, which was awkward, but it was all okay. And then I did several roles in the company in terms of product development, customer support, new business sales and marketing. And I had a good couple of years there and enjoyed it very much. but things, let's say, didn't work out in the end, and I moved on back to Epwin. pending_qa.q: What is the PLC scheme and how does it differ from other thermal performance certification databases?
pending_qa.r: The PLC scheme, which stands for Part L Compliance, was set up last year and provides approvals for energy ratings and U-values for windows and doors. Unlike other schemes that only show a company can make an A-rated window without detail, PLC details the frame, glass type, and approval specifications on the website, making it transparent and searchable with filters to find exactly what specification is needed.

pending_qa.q: How many product approvals are currently registered on the PLC scheme database?
pending_qa.r: ER Certification has several companies on the PLC scheme now, up to about 80 approval companies, with one company in particular holding over two and a half thousand approvals on the database, which customers can filter and drill down to find exactly what they need.

pending_qa.q: Why does ER Certification not engage in fire door certification despite industry demand?
pending_qa.r: Testing and certifying fire doors is a very expensive and costly undertaking. While ER Certification does certify companies manufacturing fire-rated units through cascaded data from fire glass suppliers, they are busy with window certification schemes and have sufficient growth across Europe, Poland, Lithuania, Turkey, and with American certification bodies, making fire doors not part of their current plans.

pending_qa.q: How did joining ER Certification become a turning point in a long fenestration career?
pending_qa.r: When John joined ER Certification, the potential earnings were lower than he was accustomed to, but he could see the potential. Because of his industry connections and reputation, he was able to bring clients to the business, and that first year more than doubled his expected earnings. The company has continued growing from strength to strength since then.
